title: Disinflation / Central-Bank Easing Regime: Duration, Growth, and the Classic Rotation
content: When inflation retreats toward target and central banks shift to an easing posture, fixed income duration becomes a primary return driver: the belly of the curve (3-7 years) historically captures most of the price appreciation while limiting exposure to fiscal-driven long-end volatility. Equities tend to re-rate higher on falling discount rates, but the leadership tilts toward quality large-cap growth and secular themes rather than deep cyclicals, because easing cycles are usually triggered by below-potential growth rather than boom conditions. Cash returns decay as the policy rate falls, pushing capital out of money-market instruments and into bonds and equities — a rotation that historically lifts a diversified 60/40 portfolio well above cash over the subsequent 12 months. Dollar softness frequently accompanies easing, adding a tailwind for non-dollar assets and international equity markets. The regime breaks down if disinflation stalls (re-acceleration forces a hawkish reversal) or if easing accompanies a hard landing rather than a soft one, in which case credit and equity risk should be reduced in favour of sovereign duration and defensive sectors.
lesson: In a disinflation-easing regime, extend duration into the 3-7yr belly, rotate out of cash into bonds and quality growth equities, and monitor dollar direction for international allocation signals — but watch for re-acceleration risk that would invalidate the regime.
